extracted.intended_audience: medical journal editors, editorial staff, and publishers involved in peer-reviewed medical journals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for medical journal editors on selecting, implementing, enforcing, and supporting adherence to reporting guidelines (e.g., CONSORT, PRISMA, STROBE, CARE) and related editorial policies to improve completeness, transparency, and reproducibility of published research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting completeness and transparency (methods and results)
rubrics_metrics.description: The medical literature should not mislead and should provide enough information on methods to allow replication. Methods and results should be presented with key characteristics to allow the study to be included in a subsequent systematic review/meta-analysis. Accuracy, completeness, and transparency are essential; reporting must include declaring outcomes that are prespecified or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie to ICMJE and Declaration of Helsinki. Poor reporting leads to over-optimism and patient harm and makes systematic review extraction difficult. Editors should require reporting that allows replication and systematic review inclusion; watch for outcome switching and incomplete methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requiring checklists alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Many journals recommend or require reporting checklists, but simply requiring completed checklists is not sufficient to ensure that manuscripts adhere to guidelines or that reporting quality improves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies and conference evidence show checklist submission does not guarantee adherence (authors may cite but not follow guidelines). Implementation needs enforcement, verification, and editorial processes beyond a technical checklist field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and endorse the appropriate reporting guideline(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should determine which guidelines they will endorse (eg, CONSORT, PRISMA, STROBE, STARD, CARE) and which are relevant to their journal’s content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: About 20 guidelines cover most research; hundreds of specialized guidelines exist but are less relevant for many journals. Use EQUATOR resources and searches to select appropriate guidelines and extensions for the journal’s scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide tools to help authors identify the correct guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tools such as the EQUATOR Wizard, WebCONSORT, or other checklists/wizards to help authors identify the appropriate guideline/extension for their study design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools are helpful but imperfect: some authors still misidentify the correct extension (about a third in research cited). Consider improving question sets in tools (e.g., add more questions about study features) and provide author education to reduce errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer automated and assisted checking tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt or integrate tools (e.g., Penelope, StatReviewer, combined-checklist tools, article templates) that highlight missing items or auto-fill checklists to support adherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tools can flag issues to authors and editors and can be integrated into submission systems (e.g., StatReviewer into Editorial Manager). They may reduce burden but cannot replace expert verification; they may produce false positives/negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audit the problem locally before implementing changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the journal-specific problems with reporting—who must be convinced, which shortcomings are most common, and the scale of the issue—before designing an implementation plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform an audit to measure baseline reporting quality and to identify target areas. Use audit results to build a case for change with editorial boards and publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find champions and build editorial buy-in
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify respected thought leaders and champions among editors and researchers to raise awareness and support for implementing reporting guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Champions help persuade authors and other journals; consider editorials and society meetings to publicize the initiative. Champions mitigate resistance and help communicate benefits to authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate implementation across journals in a field
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize cohorts of journals in a specialty to implement reporting guideline requirements simultaneously to prevent authors simply submitting elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint action (e.g., 28 rehabilitation journals agreeing) reduces risk of losing submissions and increases compliance. Publicize the coordinated effort with editorials and society outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide and communicate enforcement level (mandate vs recommend)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether guideline checklists are recommended, requested at revision, or mandatory at submission, and communicate that policy clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phasing in generally doesn’t work—mandate and go for it if enforcement capacity exists. Be transparent about enforcement (e.g., checklist required at submission; manuscripts without compliant checklists returned). Consider initial 'recommendation' period with clear timeline to mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical integration: require checklist upload with submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Make checklist submission a required technical element of manuscript submission (eg, selecting study type to trigger a checklist, uploading completed checklists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission-system integration (ScholarOne, Editorial Manager) can prompt authors, but beware that staff or authors may tick boxes without actual compliance. Automate where possible but ensure content verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify checklist content with subject-matter expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a content expert (methods/statistics consultant or trained editor) inspect manuscripts to confirm that checklists are completed correctly and that the reported items are present in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinicians may not know all checklist requirements. Verification requires staff time and possibly paid statisticians or methods editors; it is critical to prevent 'checkbox' compliance without substantive reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require adherence before peer review to improve review efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Require that the checklist be followed and verified prior to sending the manuscript for peer review so reviewers have the necessary information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces reviewer burden and increases the quality of peer review because reviewers can evaluate content rather than request missing methodological details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide editorial and author education and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Devise technical and educational implementation strategies at publisher and journal level; offer training packages, workshops, and examples of well-reported papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer training at meetings or virtually, produce exemplar papers, run Q&A sessions with authors, and use train-the-trainer models. Education helps authors (including those with language barriers or less experience) understand the value and use of guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate author resistance and consider author burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate pushback (authors may be displeased, shop around, or lack familiarity) and plan outreach to explain benefits and rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect complaints initially; communicate long lead times (eg, a year recommending then requiring), run outreach (editorials, society meetings), and emphasize benefits for publication success and systematic reviews. Address language and generational barriers with dedicated support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use phased operational workflow for launch, evaluation, and audit
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a written proposal, plan preparations and launch activities, then follow up with evaluation and audit of reporting quality post-implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include monitoring and audits to measure improvement (global reporting scores) and tweak processes. Continuous evaluation helps maintain uniform reporting standards rather than variable implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement specific requirements for case reports (CARE) and other article types
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and require appropriate checklists for specific article types (e.g., CARE for case reports; CONSORT, PRISMA, STROBE for trials/reviews/observational studies) and train staff/editors on common omissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case reports often miss patient history, timeline, and main take-home message; COREQ often misses details on interviewer/training/consent context. Staff should be trained to spot frequent omissions and to liaise with authors to correct them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate reporting guidance upstream (institutions, funders, registries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage broader stakeholders—institutions, funders, pre-registration platforms, publishers, and editing companies—to promote and require use of reporting guidelines at study design or funding/reporting stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders could require checklists as part of reports; institutions can provide publication officers to assist; embedding checklists into pre-registration templates may improve study design and downstream reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICMJE clinical trial data sharing statement requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: For clinical trials submitted to ICMJE journals, manuscripts must contain a data sharing statement indicating whether individual deidentified participant data will be shared; what data; related documents; when data will be available and for how long; and access criteria (including with whom, for what analyses, and by what mechanism). Trials enrolling on/after Jan 1, 2019 must include a data sharing plan in the trial registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update author instructions to reflect ICMJE timing and required content. If data sharing plans change, require updates in registry and manuscript statement. Clarify scope (deidentified participant data, data dictionaries, protocols, SAPs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship standards and contributor transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt clear disciplinary authorship standards: those who make significant intellectual contributions should be authors; identify one or more authors who assume responsibility for the entire work; require disclosure of all author roles and contributions; prohibit gift/honorary authorship, coercive authorship, ghost authorship, and omission of qualifying authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and societies should develop and publish authorship policies. Require author contribution statements and final author approvals. Work expeditiously in fields without established standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require information sufficient to reproduce results at or shortly after publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure, through policies and supporting infrastructure, that information sufficient for a person knowledgeable about the field and techniques to reproduce reported results is made available at publication or as soon as possible after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes methods detail, raw or processed data, protocols, and analysis code where possible. Use supplementary materials or data repositories; encourage or require data deposition and method transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require disclosure of all statistical tests and negative findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid unproductive duplication and permit effective judgments on statistical significance, researchers should routinely disclose all statistical tests carried out, including negative findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should support transparency of statistical testing and encourage reporting of negative results. This may require changes to instructions for authors and reviewer checklists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial registration verification to detect outcome switching
rubrics_metrics.description: Use trial registration information as part of editorial checks to determine whether prespecified outcomes were switched, demoted, omitted, or added in the manuscript compared with the registry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome discrepancies are common and can lead to biased reporting. Editors should check registry entries against reported outcomes and request clarification when discrepancies are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent reporting of demographic characteristics (race/ethnicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods should explain who classified individuals as to race/ethnicity, the classifications used, whether options were defined by investigator or participant, and reasons for assessing race/ethnicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require explicit Methods statements describing classification methods and rationale. This supports interpretation and appropriate use of demographic data in analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise sample size reporting and explicit mapping of statistical tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample sizes must be reported clearly (avoid intervals, inequalities, or nebulous phrases) and manuscripts must clearly reveal which statistical test was used for each figure or table including post-hoc tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should enforce clear numeric n values and require that Methods or figure legends map each result to the exact statistical test used. Ambiguous reporting obstructs reproducibility and should be queried during review or editorial checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policies and processes to identify and deter predatory/pseudo-journals
rubrics_metrics.description: To differentiate legitimate journals from predatory ones, journals should publish transparent editorial policies; predatory criteria used by blacklists include fake editors, plagiarized articles, and unclear peer-review policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear public editorial policies, peer-review descriptions, and contactability for editors. Monitor lists (e.g., Cabell’s) and be prepared to explain editorial practices publicly to distinguish legitimate operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial procedures for research integrity issues (EEoCs, image screening, misconduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Have processes for issuing Editorial Expressions of Concern, screening images for manipulation/duplication, and handling allegations of misconduct; many EEoCs are due to validity of data/methods/interpretation and images are a common issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider hiring technical image editors or staff to screen images before publication; maintain transparent records of EEoCs and retractions; follow COPE and institutional processes for misconduct investigations; protect whistleblowers and manage communications carefully during investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and track peer review contributions and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider formal recognition and tracking of peer review activity (institutions, funders, and ranking bodies could weight peer review contributions) and use tools to benchmark norms and verify review outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use existing tools to document review activity; advocate that institutions and funders consider peer review in promotion/funding decisions. Benchmarks are needed to assign weighting across disciplines; tracking/verification tools can help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require ORCID identifiers for authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring ORCID iDs can aid transparency and identification of authorship, and many researchers support mandating ORCID usage by publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should consider mandating ORCID IDs in submission systems to streamline author identification and disambiguation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require detailed methods (supplementary allowed) to improve reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should require detailed methodologies (including in supplementary material if print limits exist) to enable reproducibility rather than cutting methods to fit page limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider policies requiring full methods descriptions and supporting materials at publication or in repositories. For print journals, move detailed methods to supplementary files or online appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed checklists/templates into pre-registration and submission workflows
rubrics_metrics.description: Place checklist formats into pre-registration templates and submission workflows so reporting and methodological considerations are addressed earlier in the research lifecycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upstream embedding can improve study design and reporting quality. Consider integrated templates that combine multiple checklists for complex/multi-design studies to avoid duplication.
